en: *The Treatise on Resolving Doubts Concerning the One Vehicle*, by the student Zhiguī, Peng Jiqing.
I initially studied the Confucian classics, adhering rigidly to the literal text. I imitated the style of Han Yu of Changli and recklessly composed treatises to refute Buddhism.

However, I truly did not yet know what it meant for one to be a Buddha, nor what the fruit of Buddhahood was like. Subsequently, I investigated the discourse on birth and death and was suddenly awakened to a realization;
for the first time, I understood the orientation toward the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*).

Through the letters on the study of learning by various predecessors of the Song and Ming dynasties, I sought out their essential threads and gradually came to recognize the lineage of the teachings of Confucius and Yan Hui, as well as those of Mingdao, Liangshan, Yangming, and Liangxi.

The four masters were particularly devoted to their teachings, never losing them from their hearts. When they verified the principles of these four masters' profound cultivation against those of the Buddhists, they often found them to be in accord.
Among these four masters, however, only Wang Yangming did not have any explicit statements of opposition toward Buddhism.
As for the treatises composed by Mingdao, Xiangshan, and Liangxi, they sometimes cannot avoid the fault of "serving as master one moment and slave the next.

Is it because the Way of the mundane world and that of the supramundane world are inherently impossible to harmonize? Or is it because the ocean of Dharma is boundless, and few are able to exhaust its source and depths?
I harbored these doubts for a long time; only after several years did I finally resolve them. As the Lotus Sūtra says:
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third, except for what is taught through the Buddha’s skillful means.
These are merely provisional names used to guide sentient beings.

Reading the books of Confucius, I have grasped their hidden intent, and by means of the principle of "no fixed direction" from the *Appended Phrases* of the *I Ching* and the "non-reliance" of the *Zhongyong*, I have roamed the ocean-like treasury of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* throughout both the mundane and supramundane realms.
They are perfectly interfused and unimpeded. Only now do we realize that the sages of this land are for the most part great *mahā-upāya* bodhisattvas who manifest through skillful means;
yet, because their names differ, people have given rise to divergent views and engage in endless strife—is this not truly and profoundly lamentable?
Having gained confidence within myself, yet fearing the doubts of the world and posterity, I was unable to reach a definitive resolution.
Therefore, I have set forth my arguments in detail to dispel the confusion of various scholars and to exhaustively elucidate the purport of the One Vehicle.
Beyond the four masters mentioned above, there were others who openly opposed Buddhism; these are also included here for discussion.
Master Cheng said: "Buddhist learning merely uses the fear of birth and death to agitate people. The sages and worthies regard birth and death as their natural lot;
having nothing to fear, they do not discuss them. Zhi Guizi said: "If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die in the evening.
Thus, if one dies without having heard the Way, can this not be called a life lived in vain? As for those who live in vain—"
This is what the sages fear most profoundly. Therefore, one studies the *Yi* (Book of Changes) and values every passing year; one exerts oneself with such fervor that one forgets old age.
Is the concern for one’s *xingming* (nature and destiny) not truly great? When the Buddha said, "The matter of birth and death is great," he intended precisely to urge people to hear the Way.
How could he have been afraid of death? Thus it is said: "Neither born nor extinguished. This is called "one coming and going," yet in reality, there is none.
"Coming and going" is spoken of merely as the ordinary, fundamental matter of daily life.
Chengzi said: "If there were any among those in the *Chuan deng lu* who had attained realization, when facing death they would certainly seek out a cubit of cloth to wrap their heads and die;
they would by no means consent to shave their hair and wear barbarian clothing until the end. Zhiguizi said:
Phenomena do not know one another; phenomena do not reach one another. Phenomena are empty and quiescent; phenomena are equal.

Suppose one were to take a cubit of cloth and treat it as a substantial reality; would those in the world who wrap their heads in such a cubit of cloth and die thereby all be said to have heard the Way?
Among the ancients, there were indeed those who cut off their hair and tattooed their bodies yet were called masters of the Middle Way. Furthermore...

What is being said? It is that on the ground of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust is received; the four great elements are fundamentally empty—how could there be even a foot of cloth?

However, when discussing the gate of Buddha-activity (*buddhakārya*), one carries the bamboo pole wherever one goes and performs the play upon meeting the stage; such is the case with this foot of cloth.
There are many such instances. How, then, can one take what remains of my own [tradition] to disdain the deficiencies of theirs?
Chengzi said: "As for the methods of the Buddhists, their notions of loyalty, filial piety, benevolence, and righteousness are all treated as matters of necessity.
They simply wish to harmonize with [the world] by completely extinguishing the innate moral sense (*bingyi*), only then claiming it can be called the Way. However, this is ultimately...
In the end, it could not be extinguished or destroyed. Just as a person possesses ears, eyes, mouth, and nose, so too must they possess this consciousness.

That a person experiences joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure is likewise the natural state of their nature. To now insist on completely severing these in order to attain "true simplicity" (tianzhen) is, in fact, to lose true simplicity.
Zhiguizi said: "This is likely not the teaching of the Buddha. The Buddha spoke of non-attachment (*anālaya*)."
I have no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span. By practicing all wholesome dharmas, one immediately attains Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
Within the ocean of purity, there is originally not a single dharma, yet not a single dharma is abandoned.
Loyalty, filial piety, benevolence, and righteousness respond with spontaneous penetration, like an echo answering a sound; they come from nowhere and go nowhere. Furthermore:

Who could say that this is anything other than unavoidable? If one must regard the extinguishing and killing of all species as the Buddha’s sin, then one does not yet understand that among those in the world who can repay the kindness of their parents, there is truly none like the Buddha.
This so-called "Buddha" is nothing other than the perfection of awakening (*bodhi*). Because he has perfected awakening, toward all categories of sentient beings—whether born from a womb, or...
Whether born from eggs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or being formless;
whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to final liberation.
In this way, although one brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who have attained parinirvāṇa.
This is called the exhaustion of the stream of birth. To exhaust the stream of birth is to awaken all those who are children within the worlds of the ten directions.
This is called reaching the ultimate source of birth. Reaching the ultimate source of birth...
As for the source of this, it is that those throughout the worlds of the ten directions who have been fathers and mothers are all awakened together.
There is no filial piety greater than this; there is no compassion more supreme. To speak of it by way of its traces:
when King Śuddhodana was born, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); at his passing, he was reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, and Queen Māyā likewise ascended there.

The celestial palace and the sitting at the site of enlightenment—to speak of these for the sake of the youth Sudhana as the "liberation door of the illusory wisdom of the great vows of Bodhisattvas" is to cause the Buddha not to leave the royal palace and his rightful station upon the golden wheel;

it is merely to bestow glory upon those born of him so that he may receive the offerings of the ancestral temple and preserve the legacy of his descendants. Could this truly enable one to sever the wheel of birth-and-death suffering? No, indeed.

The desires of the ears, eyes, mouth, and tongue, and the emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure—if these are pursued after external objects, they are all private attachments and may be severed.
One does not sever lust, anger, and delusion, yet one does not associate with them either; there is nothing to sever.
This is called the Tathāgata, who accords with the nature of awakening. How could such a person lose their true nature? Therefore, the sanctity of a sage lies in this.
Once "will, necessity, and self" have perished, it is simply a matter of returning to the state prior to the arousal of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure;
it is nothing more than this. Master Cheng said:
"Nowadays when speaking of the Way, one must wait for a state of profound stillness and extinction, with the body like withered wood and the mind like..."
"Ashy ashes. What is truly valued is that wisdom encompasses heaven and earth and all things without omission; when has it ever been necessary to be like ashy ashes?
What is truly valued is that one’s movements and gestures accord with ritual propriety in every turn; when has it ever been necessary to be like withered wood? Zhi Gui said:
When I read the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, I then came to understand this meaning. Caoxi also said: "First, do not cling to emptiness. Chengzi said:
"The Buddha gives what is held in low esteem to others, while he himself does not practice the way of ruler and subject, father and son, or husband and wife, yet allows others to do so.
To lead people in this manner is to sever the human category. Zhiguizi said:
The realms of outflows (*sāsrava*) are formed by deluded conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Sages arise illusions from within illusion, then return to the truth from within that very illusion.
Each thing is left to itself; originally, there is not even a single thread upon which one is entangled, nor a single hair to which one clings.

The achievements of Yao and Shun are like a single speck of floating cloud passing before the eyes atop Mount Tai. Chengzi also spoke of this. Only the Buddha wishes to universally deliver the four classes of beings and lead them into...
In *nirvāṇa without remainder*, how could one ever give away what is considered base to others, causing them all to follow the Buddha’s teachings and enter *nirvāṇa* together?
It is not difficult to transform the five turbidities into a pure land; thus, the nine grades of lotus pedestals are not far from one's current location.
Forever departing from the prison of the womb, one achieves sublime adornment; why then fear being cut off from one's kind?
If it is claimed that birth from a womb is real while apparitional birth is false, one fails to realize that when the primordial chaos first opened, from what womb did the first-born person emerge?

Lice are born from the skin, and fireflies are born from grass; if this is so for the turbid, it should likewise be so for the pure. If this is so for the minute, it should likewise be so for the vast.
However, Master Cheng said: "The Buddhists reach only the point of cessation; they have no [practical] application, nor do they possess ritual propriety and righteousness. He further stated:

"Among the followers of the Buddha, there may be those who 'respectfully rectify the inner self,' but there are none who 'righteously square the outer world. Therefore, they remain stagnant and rigid."
Those who enter it become withered and emaciated; those who seek its penetration fall into license and dissipation. This is why the Buddha’s teaching is considered narrow.

It is further said that the Buddhists speak of the Way as being like looking at the sky through a tube: one strives only to go straight upward, seeing only a single direction and failing to see the four surrounding sides;
thus, they are unable to manage worldly affairs. It is also said that the Buddhists strive only for upward transcendence and lack...
This is what is studied below. Thus, how could that which is "reaching upward" (the ultimate realization) possess such [limited qualities]? Mencius said: "To exhaust the mind is to know one's nature.
This refers to what is called "recognizing the mind and seeing the nature. If one were merely "preserving the mind and nourishing the nature," these [deeper qualities] would not exist. Zhiguizi said:
"This statement by Master Cheng was intended to satirize those śrāvakas who claim their nature is fixed, as well as those reckless, deluded Chan practitioners."
He replied, "Yes. One who truly perceives the mind realizes that essence and function are one and the same, being entirely without interior or exterior.

To have an interior and an exterior is to have a place of dwelling. Because the mind is generated without a place of dwelling, it is eternally illuminating while quiescent, and eternally quiescent while functioning;

from the very beginning, it never exclusively focuses on the interior while neglecting the exterior. Thus, one strictly purifies the *vinaya* and diligently practices the six perfections, without exhausting all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

He did not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). From the beginning, he never spoke of the superior while neglecting the inferior. When Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing a wall for nine years.
Zhaozhou, apart from the two times of porridge and rice, had no other mental engagement; he nurtured and sustained [his practice] with such diligence as this.
Does one stop at knowing a single thing and consider it sufficient? For the sake of disciples of the Two Vehicles, the Buddha taught the śrāmaṇera precepts and the bhikṣu precepts.
Regarding the precepts: for the two groups of lay followers, he taught the five precepts and the eightfold fasting precepts; for the disciples of the Mahāyāna, he taught the bodhisattva precepts.
Whether broad or strict, detailed or concise, the essential aim was to cause people to act according to the station in which they reside.
One establishes preventive barriers to stop evil and promote goodness; one recognizes the mind and penetrates the root, understanding the dharma of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Devoting oneself solely to ascending directly—how could this not be true? Yet, how could there be any partiality in this? Thus, he manifested entering the mountains and demonstrated the practice of asceticism;
having already attained the Way, he dwelt in *araṇya* (forest hermitages) together with his fellow Brahmans, remaining far removed from clamor and distraction. This was truly because...
Within the burning house, one is entangled by the five desires and buffeted by the eight winds; various conditions for retrogression never cease for even a moment.

Once one enters this gate, there is absolute freedom from obstruction; hearing the Dharma, one attains the fruit and proceeds directly to Nirvana. This is the most supreme expedient for entering the Way. Thus it is said:
"The hundred craftsmen dwell in their workshops to accomplish their tasks; the gentleman studies to realize the Way."
Is it not for this reason? The teachings bequeathed by the ultimate doctrine often correspond with the words of Confucianism.

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that filial piety is named the precept; those who cultivate the practice of purity take the filial support of one's parents as the foremost field of merit, and regard a minister deceiving his sovereign or a son deceiving his father as a great evil. Other matters may generally be inferred from this. Some have said:
According to the Buddha’s teaching that all phenomena are empty, then loyalty and filial piety would both be superfluous constructs.
One must realize, however, that loyalty and filial piety are our inherent nature; they are not produced through deliberate effort.

If one understands the emptiness of all phenomena and does not allow subsequent mental constructions to turbidify this nature, then even the practice of loyalty and filial piety is merely acting without doing anything at all. How, then, could they be considered superfluous? It is as follows:
If one does not understand that all phenomena are empty, then loyalty and filial piety will conversely become fetters. Why is this?

Because being devoted to fame, stirred by emotion, and pulled by sentiment is incompatible with the pure mind. Therefore, following the Way of the Buddha, one should take its spirit as a teacher rather than becoming mired in its outward traces.

In this way, not only will one not conflict with the teachings on names and rites (*mingjiao*), but one will also provide profound assistance to them. As for the differences between [these traditions]—
Treatise: Can this not be stopped?

Master Cheng discussed hell, saying: "If even those who possess utmost sincerity—which penetrates heaven and earth—may yet fail to be transformed, how can those who establish a false teaching transform others?
He further said: "The teachings of the Śākya [Buddhists] ultimately result in deception; they begin with the world..."
They are illusory and false, yet one speaks of celestial palaces; later, one also regards these heavens as false, ultimately reducing them to nothingness.
Zhiruizi said: "If you consider the hells and celestial palaces to be products of a spurious teaching, do you mean they are not mentioned in the Six Classics?
Yet the Six Classics treat ghosts and spirits with solemnity, making them vividly clear. They possess sentience, they possess form, and they issue verbal commands and proclamations."
Ah! How majestic is the Supreme Lord! He looks down upon those below with awe-inspiring brilliance. Among humanity, he either bestows mandates upon some, or turns his gaze toward others;

to some he is full of favor, while to others he is hateful and wrathful. There is one who presides over the cycles of fortune and calamity. The Purple Microcosm is the imperial court, the domain commanded by Taiyi;
its celestial images are suspended in great clarity, shining brightly above. Is this not the evidence of the Heavenly Palace? King Wen ascends and descends [between heaven and earth].
Standing at the side of the Emperor—this is what is meant by being born into heaven. When the Duke of Zhou requested to take the place of King Wu, he said: "I am as benevolent as my father;
I possess many talents and skills, and I am able to serve the ghosts and spirits. If you say that after death there is no consciousness, then are not your words, O Duke, mere deception and falsehood?
This is like Gun becoming a bear, Peng Sheng becoming a boar, or Bo You and Hun Liangfu [becoming ghosts].
They become malevolent spirits as a result of their karmic conditions; cause and effect are without discrepancy, and this is something absolutely impossible to extinguish.
How, then, can one have any doubt regarding the hells? Indeed, all transgressions and blessings within the three realms are created by the mind alone, just as a mirror reflects images.

Beauty and ugliness reside in the person; the substance of the mirror is fundamentally empty—how could a reflection be obtained? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies that the cycle of rebirth through the seven realms of existence arises from deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), and these thoughts follow one's karma.
Within the wondrous, perfect, luminous, and effortless original mind, there is absolutely nothing to which one can cling.
Therefore, when the mind is fully understood, that which is illusory is eternally true; when one is deluded regarding the source, that which is entirely true becomes illusion.

When the Buddha says "it exists," its existence is fundamentally non-existent; when the Buddha says "it does not exist," this non-existence is itself not non-existent. Only by cutting off both existence and non-existence can the Middle Way be clearly realized.
"How could this be fathomed by those with extreme views?
Master Cheng of Yichuan said: "The Buddhists seek to eliminate affairs, yet they do not inquire whether affairs ought to exist or ought not to exist."
If it were inherently existent, how could it be set aside? If it were inherently non-existent, it would naturally be gone; what more would there be to set aside? It is further said:
Those who study the Buddha-way all wish to forget right and wrong. But how can right and wrong be forgotten? There are already so many principles; why strive to forget them?
People are merely enslaved by things, which is why they suffer and have so much business. If each thing is returned to its own place...
"Things" means to employ things. Zhiguizi said: "The teaching of 'putting affairs aside' is intended for beginners who have not yet attained fundamental clarity and are beset by many obstacles;
it causes them to temporarily cease their worldly toil and turn their light inward to reflect upon themselves.

This is what is meant by 'concentrating the mind on a single point, and there is no task that cannot be accomplished. It is a skillful means for entering the Way, but it is not the ultimate stage. (Cheng)
You have also taught people to practice quiet sitting (*jingzuo*). Is this not similar to one who withdraws from worldly affairs?
If one truly perceives the mind, it is not like this. When Śāriputra was sitting in meditation in the forest, Vimalakīrti said to him:

"As for sitting in meditation, not manifesting body or mind within the three realms—this is true sitting in meditation. Without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), yet manifesting all majestic postures..."

This is the practice of sitting in meditation (*pratisaṃlayanā*). To manifest the affairs of an ordinary person without abandoning the dharmas of the Path—this is the practice of sitting in meditation.

For the mind to dwell neither within nor without—this is the practice of sitting in meditation. To remain unmoved by all views while practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—this is the practice of sitting in meditation.
To enter into *nirvāṇa* without severing the afflictions (*kleśa*)—this is the practice of sitting in meditation. If one is able to...
Sitting in this manner is what the Buddha has sanctioned. The Great Mirror (the Sixth Patriarch) also said:
"If one wishes to achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñā*), one must attain the Samādhi of One Appearance and the Samādhi of One Practice. In all places, do not dwell upon appearances;

within those appearances, do not give rise to hatred or love, nor engage in acceptance or rejection. Do not think of matters such as benefit or ruin, success or failure. Remain at ease, tranquil, and serene."
Vast, harmonious, serene, and tranquil—this is called the Samādhi of One Characteristic.

If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely straightforward mind, remaining unmoving within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this is truly the accomplishment of the Pure Land; this is called the Samādhi of Single Practice.
When one possesses these two samādhis, what further thing could there be to exclude? As for all matters of right and wrong, they are empty and quiescent in their very essence; forget them.
Then one becomes stubborn; such attachment is also a sickness. Only with a direct mind does one harmonize with the Dharma-realm and, without giving rise to discrimination, achieve adornment.
Let each thing remain as it is—does this not lie therein? A poem says: "Without knowing, without understanding, follow the pattern of the Sovereign.
It also says: "In the silent offering, there is no contention at any time. What is there to cling to regarding right and wrong? Furthermore, what use is there for it?
"Is it not forgetting? Chengzi said:

"The Sage takes Heaven as his foundation; the Śākya [Buddhist] takes the mind as his foundation. Zhiguizi said: "To follow the timing of Heaven after it has manifested is what is called 'taking Heaven as one's foundation.
But when one precedes Heaven and Heaven does not oppose him, then upon what will he take his foundation? Qian knows the Great..."
The beginning is simply the original mind itself. Chengzi said:
"If one were to claim that the qi which has already returned will again become the qi that is about to unfold, this would be utterly unlike the nature of Heaven and Earth.
The transformation of Heaven and Earth is naturally a process of inexhaustible generation, like the rhythm of breathing; it does not require [such a forced explanation]."

"By inhaling, one produces the exhalation. It is further said that 'the wandering soul undergoes transformation. Once there is transformation, that which exists perishes and that which is solid decays;
nothing remains. Zhiguizi said: 'That which fills the space between heaven and earth is nothing but the One Spirit. Vital energy (qi) is insufficient to fully describe it.
The Spirit rides upon qi to bring forth life, just as a dragon rides upon clouds to produce rain. The clouds..."* *(Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at this point.)*
The clouds arise and vanish, yet the dragon remains as it is; the vital energy (*qi*) gathers and disperses, yet the spirit (*ling*) remains as it is.
Therefore, there are ghosts and spirits in the hidden realm, and sages in the manifest world. They preside over and regulate the Yin and Yang, and they employ and direct all moving things.
Is this caused by the vital energy becoming perverse? Or is it caused by the spirit? It must be said that it is caused by the spirit. Once the spirit acts, it can certainly not be dispersed.
It is that which perishes, like the sun and the moon. The sun of today is the very same sun as the sun of yesterday;

the moon of this month is the very same moon as the moon of last month. If they were subject to such dispersal and extinction, the transformations of heaven and earth would almost come to a standstill.
Furthermore, it is not only humans; among those that fly and those that run, and all species of wriggling creatures, there is none that does not rely upon the spirit (*ling*) for its life.
Since they have already grasped the spirit to give rise to life, none of them can be dispersed or extinguished.
Thus, the retribution for good and evil and the fruits of ascent and descent follow their natural principle; what cause for doubt could there be?
Master Cheng’s discussion on the Buddhist prohibition against killing states: "The Confucians have two theories.
One theory holds that Heaven produced birds and beasts originally for human consumption; this theory is incorrect. How could humans have been born because of lice and fleas?
Another theory holds that birds and beasts exist in dependence upon humans, and thus to kill them is unkind; this theory is also not so. Generally speaking, [it depends on] one's capacity..."
Those who overcome them may all eat them; it is only that the gentleman possesses a heart of不忍 (unwillingness to harm).

My elder brother once saw a scorpion and, unable to bear killing it, released it. Two lines in the eulogy say: "To kill it would wound benevolence; to release it would harm righteousness. Zhi Guizi said:
"If one truly knows that Heaven created birds and beasts not for human consumption, then one should embody the will of Heaven."
The mind is the mind; it is sufficient that one coexists with it without harming it. Yet you say that whatever one’s strength can overcome may be eaten.
If this logic were pursued, there would be no creature left to escape the kitchen; where, then, would the heart of compassion be?
Moreover, as for what you call benevolence and righteousness—how contradictory they are! Benevolence is the very essence of the human mind.
To act in accordance with what is appropriate is called righteousness (*yi*). To take life as benevolence (*ren*) and taking it as righteousness is fundamentally unacceptable.
A scorpion has committed no crime for which it deserves to be killed; it would be appropriate to release it. To kill it not only harms benevolence, but also violates righteousness.
Yet Master Cheng failed to examine this. Alas! I fear that people in the world will invoke righteousness as a pretext to carry out their own acts of killing.

All of these take the words of Master Cheng as their standard. Alas, how tragic it is that the learning of "the unity of all things" has fallen into ruin and the path of benevolence and righteousness has been blocked!

Zhangzi said: "If one knows that empty space is identical to qi, then existence and non-existence, concealment and manifestation, spiritual transformation, and human nature and destiny are all unified as one without duality.
If one were to claim that the myriad phenomena are merely objects perceived within the Great Void, then objects and the void would not be mutually dependent."
Form is form; nature is nature. Form and nature, as well as heaven and humanity, do not exist in mutual dependence.
To fall into the Buddhist view that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are a sickness of perception, this Way remains obscure.

This is precisely because those who are ignorant know only that the body is empty space as its nature, yet fail to realize that the fundamental Way of Heaven is its function. Consequently, they mistakenly regard the smallness of human vision and take the conditions of heaven [to be their own].
As for the realms of the manifest and the obscure, if one claims that there is no end to them, one falsely asserts that the heaven and earth of this world are mere illusions.
Failing to grasp the essential principles governing both the manifest and the obscure, one thus leaps over the proper stages and acts upon such deluded intentions. Zhiguizi said:

"In the assembly at the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, the Buddha explained to his disciples that all sentient beings have two kinds of roots. The first is the root of birth and death from time immemorial, which is—"

You who now take this攀緣心 (攀緣心, *pān-yuán-xīn*—the mind that clings to objects) as your own nature, alongside the second—the beginningless essence of Bodhi and Nirvana, which is fundamentally pure—this is precisely your current *vijñāna*-essence (*shí-jīng*, 識精), the original luminosity capable of giving rise to all conditions (*yuán*, 緣).
That which is lost amidst these conditions is due to sentient beings losing this fundamental luminosity; though they act throughout the day, they remain unaware of it, thereby wasting their lives.

Entering the various realms of existence, you do not realize that everything from the physical body outward—to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—is all an object within the wondrously luminous true mind.

It is like discarding hundreds of thousands of vast, clear oceans and recognizing only a single floating bubble, taking that bubble to be the entirety of the tide and exhausting the entire expanse of the deep seas.
You are, therefore, people who are doubly deluded. As for the "mountains" mentioned in the subsequent text...

The lands and territories of the world are all formed by the disease of vision arising from beginningless time. This is precisely because one has lost the fundamental mind and is turned about by external objects;
by grasping at preceding objects, one completely creates the cataract of vision.

This is not different from what Zhangzi criticized—that the myriad phenomena are merely objects seen within the Great Void—and that there is originally no duality between the finger and the moon. Therefore, it is said: "If you can turn objects, you will be the same as the Tathāgata."
Body and mind are perfectly luminous; this is the immovable site of enlightenment. Within a single hair-tip, one can universally contain the lands of the ten directions.

Thus, the mountains, rivers, and great earth are entirely the True within the delusive; the forms and natures of devas and humans are one and not two. The ocean-like virtues of one's nature are complete in every thought-moment.
Through this, the reason for the hidden and the manifest, and the principle of spiritual transformation, can certainly be understood. One should not...
This fragments the entire text and deviates from its original intent. Zhangzi said:
"The Buddhists speak of the great and the small, but they drift away and lose the central mean. In their exaggeration of the great, they treat the six realms as mere dust and chaff;
in their obscuration regarding the small, they regard the human world as a dream and an illusion. Can this be called 'exhausting the principle' (qiongli)? They do not know how to exhaust it."
If one acts according to principle, can it be said that one has "exhausted their nature"? To regard the six directions as mere dust and chaff is to claim that heaven and earth have limits.
To view the human world as a dream is to realize that one cannot fathom its ultimate origin. Zhi Guizi said: "That which transcends form is called the Way;
that which is below form is called the vessel. Heaven and earth are but a single vessel. Since a vessel has boundaries, it must have an end.
Huai Luo-xia’s endeavors, Da Zhang’s strides, and Shao Yao-fu’s deductions—all these are contained herein. Now, what is it that is infinite?
It is that which is above form (*rūpa*). Nature (*prakṛti*) is that which is above form.

To know that nature is infinite is to realize that one need not regard the six directions as mere dust or weeds, nor view the human world as a dream or an illusion. Thus it is said: "Ascending the East..."

"Standing on a mountain, one makes Lu seem small; ascending Mount Tai, one makes the world seem small. Zhang Zai’s criticism here also stems from a failure to discern the distinction between the Principle (Dao) and its manifestations (Qi).

To speak of the ultimate, the Principle is itself the manifestation, and the manifestation is itself the Principle; fundamentally there is neither large nor small, so how could there be arising or ceasing?
Therefore, within the tip of a single hair, one manifests the jeweled royal lands; seated within a speck of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel. All...
When beings perceive the kalpa coming to an end and being consumed by great fires, my land remains peaceful and secure, always filled with devas and humans.
Were it not for one who has realized the nature of reality, who could possibly participate in such a state?
Master Zhu said: "Within the universe, there is but one principle (li). Heaven obtains it and becomes heaven; Earth obtains it and becomes earth.
It is stretched out as the Three Bonds and regulated as the Five Constant Virtues. This principle is present everywhere and nowhere absent."
The Confucianist, in this regard, relies upon the principle of nature to achieve natural efficacy.
As for the Buddhist, they loathe this principle’s pervasive and unceasing presence, lest they find no ground of non-principle even for a single moment to rest themselves;
they detest this principle’s ceaseless circulation, lest they find no interval of non-principle even for a single breath.

At that time, they find personal satisfaction in this; thus, they rebel against their sovereign and parents, abandon their wives and children, enter the mountain forests, and sacrifice their lives to seek that which they call the realm of emptiness, non-existence, and nirvana, fleeing there. Zhirui says:

"In my previous text, I have already briefly dissected the doubts regarding the critique of 'severing kinship' and the doctrine of 'extinguishing innate human nature,' yet I have not exhausted the matter. [This is as stated in] the *Avataṃsaka*..."

There are four dharma-realms: the dharma-realm of principle (*li-fajie*), the dharma-realm of phenomena (*shi-fajie*), the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wuai fajie*), and the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wuai fajie*).
These four dharma-realms extend vertically through the three periods of time and span horizontally across the ten directions of space;
they truly may be described as filling all intervals without gap and flowing incessantly. Ordinary beings cling to existence and are deeply terrified of the emptiness of dharmas, not realizing—
The Dharma is fundamentally empty by nature, for there is nothing therein to be feared. Śrāvakas stagnate in quiescence, delighting in the departure from birth and death;

they do not know that the entire realm is their own body, for there is nothing to be departed from. This is because they fail to recognize the primordial self-nature and thus give rise to various false views, creating a separation from True Suchness (*tathatā*).
If one enters the gate of the *Avataṃsaka*’s vast, perfectly interfused, and unimpeded teachings, one accords with the emptiness of all phenomena and gives rise to...

The Great Wisdom-Vow moistens all things and benefits all beings. It penetrates deeply into both the mundane and supramundane realms, appearing and disappearing according to conditions, yet without any agent;
it is simply the natural state of reality (*dharmatā*), beyond all conceptual thought.
Therefore, while Vairocana pervades all places, his manifestation as a bhikṣu preaching the Dharma is merely one aspect of Śākyamuni’s responsive transformations (*nirmāṇa*). [He] enters...
In the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," the youth Sudhana visits spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) one after another;

some appear in the form of a king to preach the Dharma for him, while others appear in the form of an elder or a lay devotee to preach the Dharma for him. This is what is meant by "unimpeded" [wisdom].

Thus, it may be said that the Sages Yao, Shun, and King Wen of Zhou were but single manifestations among the hundreds of thousands of millions of transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya). This refers to their manifestation...
He preached the Dharma while manifesting in the body of a king of men.

It may be said that Confucius was one of his thousands of millions of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), appearing in the form of an elder or a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) to preach the Dharma. He established the three cardinal relations and maintained the five constant virtues.
Encompassing heaven and earth, they accomplish all things through their subtle workings;

they take the entire great chiliocosm and weave it together as a fabric, yet this never fills even one ten-millionth part of a single pore of Samantabhadra. Why is this? Because principle is inexhaustible, phenomena are likewise inexhaustible;
because phenomena are inexhaustible, practice is likewise inexhaustible. Precisely because they are inexhaustible, they are unimpeded. What weariness could there be? What aversion could there be?
There is. Regarding Zhu Xi’s discussion on observing the mind, he said: "The mind is that by which a person presides over the body.
When used to observe external things, the principles of those things are apprehended. Now, if there were another thing to reflect back upon this mind, then this mind—"
Beyond the mind, there is yet another mind that is able to govern this mind. Thus, one seeks the mind with the mind, and employs the mind by means of the mind;
it is like using the mouth to bite the mouth, or the eye to look at the eye. Zhinaguizi said:
"To claim that one contemplates objects with the mind is to seek objects externally with the mind. To claim that one contemplates the mind with objects is to seek the mind externally with objects."
Furthermore, the mind has no interior or exterior; therefore, phenomena have no interior or exterior. Because phenomena have no interior or exterior, contemplation has no interior or exterior.
Thus, it is appropriate to seek the mind with the mind, just as empty space joins with empty space.
It is also appropriate to employ the mind with the mind, just as the body employs its arm. Did not the ancient masters say: "Who is this person who contemplates? What is this mind?"
Regarding the matter, Zhu Xi replied to Lian Songqing: "What is called the 'nature of Heaven and Earth' is precisely my own nature.

How could there be such a principle as it suddenly perishing upon death? One who does not understand this teaching—does he take Heaven and Earth as the primary subject, or does he take me as the primary subject?"
It depends on what you take as the "Master. If you take Heaven and Earth as the Master, then this nature is simply one universal principle within Heaven and Earth;
although it is said that "though one dies, it does not perish," it is nonetheless not something that can be privately possessed by a self.
If you take the self as the Master, then it is merely recognizing a spirit, soul, and vitality endowed with consciousness within one's own person.
Regarding things that possess consciousness, one immediately regards them as one's own nature, grasping and manipulating them until death, refusing to let them go.

Claiming that they die but do not perish is the height of selfish intent. How could such a person be worthy of being discussed about the doctrine of life and death or the principle of *xing* and *ming*?
If it were truly so, then within the single nature of Heaven and Earth, there would be a separate...
There are various natures among human beings. Each nature has its own boundaries and does not intermingle with others.

They are born and die of their own accord, rather than being created by Heaven and Earth or Yin and Yang; furthermore, even Heaven, Earth, Yin, and Yang have no means of exercising their creative power over them.
How could such a principle exist? Zhin gui zi said: "To take Heaven and Earth as the primary agents [is incorrect]."
To claim that [the self] depends on me is called the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

Not knowing that once "no-self" is realized, who would name heaven and earth, and who would be imperishable—to take "me" as the master and not to depend on heaven and earth—is called the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

Not knowing that the perception of a self is the very root of birth and death, for within the true and eternal nature there is neither "that" nor "I"—due to the former views, the sages of the world at first...
There is no such teaching. The *Lunyu* says: "If you do not yet know life, how can you know death? This means that there is no dual principle between life and death. It further says:
"If you have not yet been able to serve living humans, how can you serve the spirits? This means that there is no difference in the nature of humans and spirits.

It is clear, therefore, that one must not attempt to fathom these matters through the lens of nihilistic views (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). From this subsequent perspective, even the supramundane sages have no such teaching.
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Those who have attachment to self also love nirvāṇa; suppressing the root of attachment to self is called the mark of nirvāṇa.
Those who have aversion toward self also loathe birth-and-death; because they do not realize that attachment to self is true birth-and-death, they separately loathe birth-and-death."
This is called non-liberation. It is certain that one cannot seek it through the view of permanence;
rather, when the two views are decisively severed, arising and ceasing are equal, and going and coming are as one—this is what is called true liberation.

How could it be a matter of grasping and manipulating while refusing to let go? As for the nature of sentient beings and things, although they originate from the same source, their manifestations diverge.

They are distinct. It is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers; though each river has its own moon, the clarity and turbidity are separated, and the brightness and darkness are vastly different.
How could one say that because the single moon is the same, the thousand rivers have no distinction? Although every river is distinct, what impediment is there to the sameness of the single moon?

Since it is so with birth, why should there be doubt regarding death? In the transformative workings of Yin and Yang, the spirit is moved and the spirit responds; this is also the case for all things.
It is merely a matter of each person’s own endowment; from the beginning, how could there have ever been any intentional interference therein?

Zhu Xi said: "The Buddhists polish until the mind becomes extremely refined, like a piece of material from which one layer of skin is stripped off, then another layer, until it is polished to the absolute limit where nothing more can be stripped away. Thus they grind it down.
This is the luminous essence of the mind. He, however, mistakenly identifies this as "nature" (*xing*). Little does he realize that this is precisely what the Sage calls the "mind.
The Buddhists originally did not recognize this principle; instead, they identify cognitive awareness and movement as nature, such as seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting.
To the Sage, however, there is a principle of seeing inherent in seeing, a principle of hearing inherent in hearing, and a principle of speaking inherent in speaking.
Movement possesses the principle of movement; thought possesses the principle of thought. These are what are called clarity, acuity, compliance, reverence, and sagacity.
The Buddhists, however, identify that which is able to see, hear, speak, think, and move as being the very nature (xing).
Whether horizontal or vertical, they recognize all of these as nature. They most fear the word "principle" (li), seeking to eliminate it entirely.

This is precisely what is meant by the doctrine that "the nature of the child at birth is called nature. Zhiguizi said: "Seeing, hearing, speaking, and appearance do not exist outside of the one mind.
The essence of this one mind is what is called *ruì* (profound sagacity). It is truly as it has been said: 'Strip away one layer, then strip away another layer;
when they are stripped away completely, the light of Heaven returns. Once the light of Heaven has returned, the Heavenly principle manifests of itself. To see..."
Listening, seeing, speaking, and acting flow forth from this [One Mind]. They are naturally clear, intelligent, reverent, and compliant, never overstepping their proper measure.

Is this not indeed the achievement of sagehood? If there were a principle of seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting that existed apart from this One Mind, how could one say that "one thread runs through them all"?
As the Patriarch’s verse says: "In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing; in the nose it is called smelling..."

Fragrance is in the mouth when one speaks, in the hands when one grasps, and in the feet when one runs; it manifests everywhere, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm, yet can be withdrawn into a single atom.
Those who recognize this know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*jīng-hún*).
The verse points directly to the fact that once the One Mind is realized, there are no other dharmas. To "recognize" (*shí*) requires great skill; it is just as the Confucians speak of "recognition."

As for the purport of benevolence (*ren*): once one has applied effort for a long time, the fundamental luminosity will be revealed—tranquil, quiescent, and eternally true, pervading all realms as numerous as grains of sand.

This is what is called "knowing the mind" and is also termed "seeing the nature. It is precisely this that is meant by the saying: "If for a single day one can overcome the self and return to ritual propriety (*li*), the whole world will turn to benevolence.
As for the two characters "mind-nature," they originally have no fixed definition; even within Confucian discourse, they already differ from one another.
Mencius said, "Benevolence (ren) is the human mind. Some speak of it as the "original mind" (benxin), while others speak of it as the "good mind" (liangxin).
When has it ever been exclusively defined as the faculty of cognition and movement? The Master [Confucius] said, "Human nature is nearly the same," and Mencius spoke of the goodness of nature;

both must be verified through human feelings (qing). When has there ever been a discussion of nature that is divorced from the mind? The Buddhists speak of the mind, distinguishing between the "true mind" (zhenxin) and the "deluded mind" (wangxin).
Regarding "nature," there is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
How could it ever be that [the mind] takes only cognition and movement as its nature? In essence, the nature of the mind is merely a provisional designation.

It is established through skillful means (*upāya*) to deliver the deluded masses. If one reaches the fundamental source and forgets all attachments, one will not even perceive a person who realizes, nor an object realized.
Regarding the Dharma, how could one arbitrarily form subjective opinions and recklessly judge right and wrong? Within the gateway of Buddha-activity, one must rely upon established principles;
therefore, the categories of the Five Precepts embody the entirety of the Five Constant Virtues, and the articles of the Ten Wholesome Paths encompass all five matters.
How could there be a teaching that posits a principle external to these? As for the discourse on the "sweeping away" found in the Chan school, it is like the medicinal pair of *dahuang* and *fuzi*.
My son, we seek only to eliminate illness; what harm is there in the initial dizziness and nausea? To kill someone through an error is not the fault of the medicine itself.
How can one condemn the founder of the teaching on account of the abuses that arise from its later practitioners?
Zhu Xi said: "Of the Buddhist scriptures, only the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* is an ancient text; the rest were all refined and composed by Chinese scholars.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* was also produced by people of the Northern and Southern Dynasties. He further remarked:
"Before Bodhidharma came to China, those such as Master Huiyuan and Daoshao spoke only of Laozi and Zhuangzi. Later generations likewise mostly [relied on] Laozi..."

Zhuangzuo’s commentary on Chan: How could there be tonal prosody in the Western Regions? The verses transmitted by the various patriarchs that harmonize level and oblique tones were all composed by later people.
Furthermore, it is said: "The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* has only three sections that are good; the rest is merely forced additions.
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* was originally nothing but mantras, but later Fang Rong added many discourses on principles. [Mantra]
Their linguistic concepts are also shallow and superficial. However, their followers feared that if these were translated, people would easily understand them; therefore, they did not translate them.

They further claimed, "The Buddha merely speaks grandiloquent lies to deceive people; the Lotus Sūtra opens with talk of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges], tens of thousands of kalpas, and thousands of kalpas, with no dates from recent times.
Zhi Guizhi said: "In India, there is only the Brāhmī script."
When entering this land, one must necessarily rely upon a Dharma Master for translation. Such a Master must be proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit;
only then can they employ the literary expressions of this region to expound the Buddha’s intent. As for the fact that the verses possess harmonious rhyme, why should there be any doubt?

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* were translated by Kumārajīva; the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Yuanjue jing*) was translated by Buddhatrāta; and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* was translated by Paramiti.
Regarding the translation by Miti: at that time, the literary scholars were not proficient in Sanskrit script; how could they have known the Buddha’s intent and polished it into its final form?
Only the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* was transcribed by Fang Rong. To say "transcribed" (bi-shou) merely means recording and proofreading;
it does not imply the ability to add anything new. If the scripture had truly emerged from Rong’s own hand, why would he have concealed the fact that he translated it himself?
While names must necessarily rely on Indian monks to establish their authority, as for mantras—which are esoteric speech—one merely adopts the sounds without adopting the meanings;
this is common to all scriptures, where it is said that because they are shallow and mundane, they are not translated. Could this really be so?

The purport of the Buddha’s scriptures is fundamentally distinct from that of Laozi and Zhuangzi. Laozi says, "The Way takes nature as its law," whereas the Buddha speaks of "subtle awakening and wondrous luminosity."
It is neither cause nor condition; it is neither spontaneous nor non-spontaneous; it is neither "not" nor "not-not"; it is neither "is" nor "is-not. Laozi said:
"Vague and indistinct—within it there is form. Indistinct and vague—within it there is substance. The Buddha, however, says:
"Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, this would still be the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmas*)."

Regarding the matter of shadows: Zhu Xi also remarked that the followers of Laozi still concern themselves with their own single body, whereas the followers of Śākyamuni do not attend to the body at all.
While Zhuangzi’s method of annihilation is incomplete, the Buddha’s annihilation is total. Now, when Laozi says, "By regarding the body as external, the body survives;
by placing the body last, the body takes precedence," he has still not succeeded in transcending the body. The Buddha, however, realizes that the aggregates (skandhas) are non-existent.
I am the body that is no-body; this body that is no-body is called the Great Body, and it is called the Body Pervading the Dharma-realm.

As for "utter extinction," this does not refer to withered wood or dead ashes. When the delusions of the three realms are exhausted and the myriad virtues are fully perfected, what surplus dharma could there be within the Constant, Quiescent Light?
This is something that even Bodhisattvas of the Tenth Ground cannot fathom to the end, let alone those of the Voice-hearers.
Hearing this, the various non-Buddhists and the people of the Southern and Northern Dynasties claimed that their own wisdom surpassed that of Laozi and Zhuangzi.

However, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "This Dharma cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination. The length of kalpas and eons arises from the limited measures of the human mind.
When the measure of emotional conditions is exhausted, long and short are as one. Therefore it is said: "I observe the distant past as if it were today.

These words, which accord with the nature of reality, how could they be mere empty talk? The *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment* and the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* first reveal the self-nature of true emptiness and subsequently manifest the rules for cultivation.
They encompass both the sudden and gradual approaches; they are good in the beginning, middle, and end. This is the definitive realm of the Tathāgata. This is...
The Buddhas of the ten directions have all emerged through the single gate of the Path of Sublime Adornment; how can one harbor a mind of contempt and arrogance to recklessly slander them?

Lu Ji’s judgment of Confucianism and Buddhism lies in the distinction between righteousness and profit, and the public and the private. Only by adhering to righteousness and the public good can one govern the world.

Because their benefit is solely for oneself, [the Confucians] seek transcendence from the world; though the Confucianist reaches the state of being "without sound or smell, without form or substance," they all take the governance of the world as their primary concern.
Though the Buddhist seeks to universally deliver beings throughout the limits of the future, they all take transcendence from the world as their primary concern.
Zhiguizi said: "No, no. It is not that the Confucians have never governed the world, nor that the Buddhists have never transcended the world.

What are called the 'world' and the 'transcendent world' are merely what the discriminating mind perceives. The great men of antiquity transformed all they passed by and preserved their spiritual essence within themselves;
though they possessed the empire, they did not cling to it, and though their virtue covered the four seas and their merit lay with the myriad generations..."
In the beginning, the world had never seen the existence of a "ruling over all under heaven.

If one were to insistently take the governing of the world as their primary concern, this would mean they already possess the world and participate in it; this is selfishness, and it is the employment of clever intelligence.
Its scope and substance are vast, and its fame and influence are manifest; yet such a person is not fit to speak with Fuxi, Huangdi, or Yao.

It is certain that the minds of Shun and King Wen were like this. What the Buddha calls "transcending the world" means to transcend the world of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) and the world of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
To speak more precisely, what is called "the world" is nothing other than the mind of arising and ceasing.
This is what the *I Ching* refers to when it says: "With a restless coming and going, your thoughts follow after your friends. It is the emotion of arising and ceasing.
When [the mind] is exhausted, one transcends the world. This means that by means of the mind of arising and ceasing, one awakens to the mind of true permanence.

"It stops at the back; one does not perceive one's own body. One walks in the courtyard; one does not see the people there. This is what it refers to. That is, by means of the mind of arising and ceasing, one awakens to the mind of equality.

"The world returns to the same destination by different paths; it reaches the same unity through a hundred deliberations. What is there for the world to think about? What is there to deliberate? This is what is meant.
Until one reaches this state, that which is called "governing the world" is merely a matter of petty pleasure and minor remedies;
that which is called "transcending the world" is merely the path of the Śrāvaka and the Hīnayāna. How great, then, is their self-interest and pursuit of gain!
"Ah! Lu Ji said:
'Although the followers of Śākyamuni have left the household life, they also repay the four debts of gratitude.
Amidst their daily lives, this principle remains rooted in their hearts and cannot be extinguished; they certainly preserve it therein. However, as for their teaching, it is not...'"
It arises for the sake of preserving this [mind-nature]. Therefore, whether it is preserved or not is insufficient to weigh the relative importance for one who has deeply penetrated the Way.
If we Confucians were to say: "That by which humans differ from birds and beasts is but slight;
the common people discard it, while the noble person preserves it," then that which the Buddhists pity is simply the failure to escape saṃsāra, where birth and death alternate.

Continuing: this refers to floating and sinking within the sea of birth and death. Yet, among our Confucian sages and worthies, how could they all merely be floating and sinking within that sea of birth and death?
That which they pity and compassion for, we sages and worthies do not possess.
However, that teaching was not formulated for the purpose of avoiding this [concern], and thus its exposition does not primarily center upon it.
Zhiguizi said: "Of all phenomena in the myriad dharmas, there are none that are not established from within one's own mind. The essential point lies in knowing the root;

once the root is attained, one need not worry about the branches. Therefore, it is said: "Vast and expansive, deep and springing forth, it emerges at the proper time. The entire book *Zhongyong* [is based on this principle].

Heaven’s Mandate established the school, taking the "soundless and scentless" as its ultimate destination. In its discourse on learning, it distinguishes between those who know by birth, those who learn to know, and those who know through hardship;
it differentiates between those who act with ease, those who act with benefit, and those who act through exertion. Yet they all return to the One. What is this One?
It is what is called the "Fundamental. To "know" is to know this; to "act" is to realize this. This is knowledge.
The root is clarity; to reach the root is sincerity. Being sincere and clear is nothing more than the unceasing operation of the Way of Heaven.
It is beyond the power of words to fully describe it. Extending this to human relations and applying it to all things, one acts without any doubt.

Therefore, by not practicing [anything], there is nothing that is not beneficial. Through profound reverence, the world is brought to equilibrium. In reality, there is not a single dharma to be grasped; thus it is said:
"The workings of the High Heaven are without sound and without smell—how ultimate! Lu Ji said:

"If a person does not fully realize the Way of Humanity, they are insufficient to stand alongside Heaven and Earth. I also say: "If a person does not comprehend the Way of Heaven, how can they precede Heaven?"
Yet Heaven does not oppose him. How could one who is able to encompass Heaven and Earth and complete all things in their particularity have failed to grasp the fundamental?
Among the nine schools of thought, the miscellaneous masters, and the myriad crafts and arts, there is none that does not fall within the scope of this encompassing and completing.

Why, then, should one treat only the Buddha as being outside of this? To harbor a mind that excludes others is insufficient for attaining the Way of Heaven; and failing to attain the Way of Heaven, [one cannot truly understand it].
"It is impossible for one to be able to transcend birth and death and sever the cycle of saṃsāra [merely by such means].
Master Jingzhai said: "Buddhist learning consists simply in adhering to a single path and not further exhausting oneself investigating the principles of the world.
Therefore, its study is easily mastered; one merely maintains a single state of mind and proceeds directly toward Buddhahood. It is not like..."
The Confucian’s wisdom encompasses all things and his Way benefits the world, yet his mind remains constant. For the Confucian, the mind and principle are one and thus persist;
for the Buddhist, the mind and principle are separate and thus persist. Zhiguizi said: "Principle is neither localized nor omnipresent; it is simply a matter of awakening.
If one is constantly awakened, there is no principle that is not fully realized, and whatever is applied at any given moment will be appropriate. If...
To regard principle as having an external existence and to guard it with the mind—this is duality. The Confucianist is cautious and reverent when not looking, and fearful when not hearing;
there is nothing that does not return to the root in solitude. The Sage uses this to wash his heart and withdraws to hide within the profound mystery.
Furthermore, there has never been one who did not take a single thought as the ground for their practice.
To abandon the single thought and seek it elsewhere among the myriad phenomena is like having no root or no source water; how could one hope to avoid withering and drying up?

For this reason, Confucius silently took note of it, Yanzi seemed to have something established within him, Mencius sought to recover the lost mind, the Duke of Zhou emphasized stillness, and Cheng Yi emphasized... (the text is incomplete).
Jingyan said: "Meditating silently to clarify the mind and embody the Heavenly Principle—this is precisely what this aspiration [of mine] is about.
To have awakening regarding this is called 'knowing the root. To have no object of awakening is called 'reaching the root. To seek the Way apart from this is entirely to be a heterodox path.
To harbor the mind while seeking the Principle is called 'losing the mind.'"

Master Hu said: "To have no shame even under the roof or in the corner of a room means that although there may not be a single thing manifest, the myriad principles are already present in their full array within.
This is the substance (ti), though it has simply not yet been aroused. To regard this as empty and non-existent, as the Daoists and Buddhists do, is to sever the fundamental substance."
People nowadays merely say that Laozi and the Buddha have substance but lack function. I maintain that this is precisely because their substance was already severed within;
therefore, they have no function without. Zhiguizi said: "The Fangguang (Vaipulya) non-Buddhists establish the doctrine of emptiness and non-action, which is rejected by the Buddhist teachings.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: 'It is better to hold a view of a person as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the notion of nothingness.'"
Regarding the empty view of those with overweening pride, Caoxi said: "The world is like space; it can contain the forms and images of all things:

the sun, moon, and stars; mountains, rivers, and the great earth; springs, sources, streams, and ravines; grasses, trees, thickets, and forests; evil people and good people; evil dharmas and good dharmas; heavens and hells;
the entire great ocean, Mount Sumeru, and all other mountains—all are contained within this space. Thus it is for the people of the world.
The emptiness of nature is likewise so. The measure of the mind is vast and great, pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm.
When its function is active, it is clear and distinct; when applied, one immediately knows all things. All is one, and one is all.

Coming and going are free and unimpeded, for the essence of the mind dwells nowhere. This is called Prajñā. For this reason, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva made the ten great kings of vows, saying: "Empty..."

When the realm of space is exhausted, when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, when the karma of sentient beings is exhausted, and when the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted, only then will my vow be exhausted.
Does this mean that there is a substance but no function? Or rather, that there is neither substance nor function? Furthermore, regarding what you call "the dense array already complete":
does this mean it is complete within emptiness itself? Or does it exist separately from emptiness? If it exists separately from emptiness, then where would it reside?
If it is already present within emptiness, why disparage emptiness? It is simply that one must not harbor attachment to emptiness.

Master Hu said: "The Confucianist maintains the mind through reverence; the substance of that mind remains serene within the physical frame, like a master of the house staying at home, able to manage household affairs.
This is a living master. The Buddhist sits in silence to clarify [the mind]..."
The mind: set aside all thoughts and deliberations until, after a long time, it reaches a state of empty vacuity; this is the absence of a master.
Furthermore, there are those who merely bind and restrain the mind to force it to remain; they kill it outright, rendering it unable to act as its own master. This is the inferior form of Chan.
True emptiness and the absence of mind—this is the superior form of Chan. Guizhi said: "The mind has no fixed location."
If there were a cavity to be sought and a state of limpid clarity to be pointed out, it would be merely a solidified object;
what else could it be but dead and inert? Even "true emptiness" and "no-mind" are not yet ultimate. As the ancient masters said: "Originally there is mind."
To lack this mind is to fall entirely into slander. They judge existence and non-existence based on their own opinions; how could they possibly differ by less than a thousand li?
Master Hu said: "The Buddhist's vision of the Way is like Emperor Wu of Han seeing Lady Li—it is not a true vision."

The Śākyas merely speculate about principles; therefore, they labor in vain without achieving results. The Confucians, however, investigate things directly within the realm of phenomena. Zhiguizi said:
"Since the learning of 'investigating things' (gewu) has not been clearly understood, many people have taken the mere 'expanding of the mind' to be their study.
Regarding the discussion of investigating things in the *Great Learning*, the preceding text states: "Things have their root and their branch."
All affairs have a beginning and an end. To know what comes first and what comes last is to be close to the Way. This means that the root comes first and the branches come last.
The subsequent text clarifies the distinction between the root and the branches, concluding: "This is called knowing the root; this is called the ultimate of knowledge."

The *Ming* (Awakening) states that to know one’s foundation is the pinnacle of knowledge. What is this foundation? It is the luminous virtue (*mingde*). To know the foundation is to know where to rest.
Among the merits of investigating things (*gewu*), nothing is more essential than this. How could it ever have been taught that one should seek exclusively within external phenomena?

The *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* says: "Thoroughly investigate the wondrous luminosity; observe without ceasing. "Thoroughly investigating" is precisely what the Confucian tradition calls "investigating and extending knowledge" (*gewuzhi*). As for "observing"...
As for "investigation," this is what the Confucians mean by "constantly bearing it in mind. In the School of the Gate (Buddhism), one must first engage in thorough inquiry;
after long application of effort, there comes a moment of sudden clarity—this is called "seeing one's nature. How could one ever take mere mental imagination to be the Way?
Master Hu said: "The Buddhists claim that death is a return to the True. Yet they fail to realize that birth has its own principle of arising, which cannot be said to be non-existent.
By regarding death as a return to the True, they thereby treat life as unreal. Zhiguizi said: "The Buddha taught that through the harmony of causes and conditions, there is illusory birth;
through the separation of causes and conditions, what is illusorily called 'extinction' occurs. [The Buddhists] simply do not understand this."

Arising and ceasing, going and coming—the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading; it is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within this true and eternal nature, if one seeks arising and ceasing, delusion and awakening, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found. Such are these sincere words.

To part the clouds and see the sun—how could one ever, within the phenomena of arising and ceasing, forcibly give rise to acceptance or rejection? "To live as a guest and return as a corpse" is a common worldly saying;
even upon consulting the Buddhist scriptures, such a thing has never been heard before.

Someone asked: "The Buddhists claim that the true nature (zhenxing) is neither born nor extinguished; what is the meaning of this? Master Hu said: "The Buddhists take consciousness and movement as the mind (*citta*).
This is simply the locus of the spirit of *qi*. Therefore, they strive to maintain control over this thing in order to avoid the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
For this reason, I say that the Buddhists do not recognize the nature; they falsely point to the spirit of *qi* and call it the nature. Knowledge.
Guizi said: "Neither arising nor ceasing, its fundamental substance is thus. It perfectly encompasses the six voids, and there is nothing else besides it.

Perception, cognition, movement, and activity—what among these is not the mind? Fundamentally, it has no place of abiding; why then should one grasp at it? If you mistake the vital breath for the mind,"
This immediately becomes a bond; it is the root of birth and death.

What, then, is called true nature? Jingyang Gu Zhi said: "The Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures—if one were to summarize them in a single phrase, it would be: 'neither good nor evil.
Try examining the gāthās of the Seven Buddhas and you will see for yourself. Someone else said: "The *Song of Realizing the Way* by Yongjia speaks of discarding existence..."
To cling to non-existence (*wu*) is like abandoning a drowning man only to throw oneself into a fire; I fear that the Buddha’s school does not necessarily take non-existence as its fundamental tenet.

[The opponent] says: "This is merely playing with the four characters 'neither good nor evil' to the very end; there is no other meaning. To discard existence is because one regards existence as evil;
to cling to non-existence is because one regards non-existence as good. This is still to have good and evil; non-existence, too..."
Do not cling; do not even discard existence. Then there will be neither good nor evil. From this point onward, push away stage by stage;
sweep again and again until nothing whatsoever remains. All of it is simply this very state of mind. Zhiguizi said:
"Good and evil are names of relative opposition that take form in response to external objects. Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect."
The essence is inherently empty and quiescent; it cannot be designated by "existence" or "non-existence," much less by "good" or "evil.
When Mencius spoke of human nature, he said: "As for its emotional dispositions, they are capable of being good. This was a statement that human nature is capable of being good.
Master Cheng said: "That which precedes 'the stillness with which humans are born' cannot be described. As soon as one speaks of 'nature,' it is no longer nature itself.
To name nature by means of good and evil—all such [definitions] are what Master Cheng called 'not nature. This involves abandoning one thing while clinging to another."
This is merely following after external objects; it is not the fundamental nature of reality. Therefore, one who knows this nature does not grasp at a single dharma, yet there is nothing abandoned;
nor does he reject a single dharma, yet there is no attachment. Sweep again and sweep again until all is cleared away.
When everything has been swept clean, the two extremes are severed, and the perfect awakened mind pervades the entire universe. It is like the sun appearing when the clouds disperse.
The source being profound, the stream is long; it flows straight down with transparent clarity, leaving no further dharma behind.
This is the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the primary exposition of all the Sages. As for the gates of skillful means (*upāya*), they do not abandon the application of remedies;

for when the Dharmakāya accords with conditions to give rise to various defiled dharmas, one must rely upon the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to perfect its pure function. Therefore, regarding practice, it is essential...

As [the practice] gradually fulfills its course, one should expect the gradual severance of delusions. Only by cultivating the six perfections in unison and perfecting all myriad virtues can one purify the various buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity.

As the Sūtra says: "In principle, there is sudden awakening; through awakening, [delusions] are simultaneously extinguished. In phenomena, there is no sudden elimination; they are exhausted through successive stages.
Once you recognize that the essence of good and evil is fundamentally empty, what obstacle could hinder your cessation of evil and performance of good? Until you reach the ultimate...
The ground of goodness. Who can testify that the root of good and evil is ultimately investigated? The root of good and evil is fundamentally empty; this is sudden awakening in principle (*li*).

Ceasing evil and practicing good—this is not suddenly eliminated in phenomena (*shi*). When truly extinguished, it is truly exhausted; when truly exhausted, it is truly extinguished. Without lingering on the middle path, one proceeds directly to the precious abode.
If one clings to principle while neglecting phenomena, or pursues phenomena while losing sight of principle, how could such a person be fit for discussion?
This is indeed the finger-pointing to the non-obstruction of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra!
I said to you: "Soundless and odorless" is what our Confucian tradition calls emptiness; "neither good nor evil" is what the two [non-Buddhist] traditions call emptiness.
Their names appear similar, yet their realities are far apart. Therefore, those who avoid speaking of emptiness do so because they discard it due to these superficial similarities.
"True. As for those who confuse the words and speak of emptiness, they use the semblance to disorder the truth; I dare not claim to know them. Zhi Guizi said: 'Emptiness is one and only.
If one claims that the absence of sound and smell implies the existence of good and evil, then it cannot be called the absence of sound and smell.
If one claims that the absence of good and evil implies the existence of sound and smell, then it likewise cannot be called [the absence of sound and smell].'"
There would be neither good nor evil. For sound and odor are the germination of good and evil; good and evil are the manifestation of sound and odor.
To take what is good in order to distinguish it from emptiness is just like taking what exists while avoiding emptiness.

I wonder, does your intention not hold that having good and lacking evil constitutes true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), whereas having neither good nor evil ultimately leads to a state of chaotic indistinctness? To regard this as...
The profound chasm separating Confucianism and Buddhism arises from a failure to understand the texts of the *Great Changes* (*Da Yi*).

When it is said that [the Dao] is "empty" and "silent," "without form or substance," and "beyond thought or deliberation," how could goodness be something that can be possessed? The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:

"Though one knows that the lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates pure lands and teaches and transforms sentient beings. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: [and so forth].
When this bodhisattva cultivates all roots of goodness, they form this thought:
"May the power of the merit of these roots of goodness reach every place— just as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) reaches nowhere—
