it reaches all things, reaches all worlds, moves among all sentient beings, reaches all lands, reaches all phenomena, and reaches the One."
From all of empty space to all of the three periods of time; reaching all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;
reaching all languages and sounds—may these roots of goodness likewise be so. Goodness is attainable yet without deviation.

One must simply sit and sever existence and non-existence, remaining far removed from emptiness and form. Before a single thought arises, ten thousand virtues gather universally. Amidst the profuse manifestation of great function, right where one is...
Quiescence—this is ultimate true emptiness (*tathatā*). Why then do you fall into such biased and chaotic extremes?
As for those who grasp at goodness and block out emptiness, or grasp at emptiness and abandon goodness, their minds remain untransformed and their frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) increases.

They not only deviate from the school of the Three Contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) of the Śākya gate, but how could they possibly understand the teaching of "non-speaking" (*avaktavya*) of the Master Kong [Confucius]?
One day, while out for a stroll visiting Guanyin Temple, Gu Zi saw men and women traveling along the road, passing back and forth in an unending stream.
He said to his younger brother, Ji Shi: "This alone is sufficient to distinguish between Confucianism and Buddhism. This is precisely why [the latter] does this."
It is merely a matter of a single mind regarding fortune and calamity. I have never seen anyone who, for the sake of seeking fortune or avoiding calamity, sought out our Sage.
How could the Buddha ever have invited him to come? How could our Sage ever have rejected him to make him go?

How could the Buddha ever have spoken exclusively of fortune and calamity? How could our Sage ever have avoided speaking of fortune and calamity? Examine this within the context of these words. Between them...
"There must be a segment of true spirit that stands apart and is fundamentally different. Ji Shi said, "This is merely what foolish men and women do;
those with discernment would certainly not act thus. [The Master] said, "When such resonance reaches even the level of foolish men and women..."
Only when its resonance is genuine does its response reach even the most ignorant of men and women; only then is its response truly authentic.
As for the term "genuine" (*zhen*), it means being purely of Heaven (*tian*) and having no admixture of the human (*ren*). Zhiguizi said: "Alas!
The hearts of the ignorant masses are perhaps not merely moved by blessings and calamities. For they are close to..."
Among those capable of bringing about calamity or fortune for human beings, none are more influential than the deities of the city walls and local village altars.
Yet, these deities of the city walls and village altars can only move the people of their respective districts and towns.

On a larger scale are the deities of the rivers, streams, seas, and mountains, who produce clouds and rain and manifest strange phenomena. Even greater than these are the deities of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations.

They preside over transgressions and blessings, and govern birth and death; thus, officials report to them, and those with petitions pray to them—they are merely able to move the people of a particular region and bring them to rest.
As for the reach of the Buddha’s transformation, it is vast and boundless, without end or limit.
How could it be limited to such things as calamity and fortune? Truly, it is said that he realizes the Dharma-nature body, exhausts the root of ignorance, and moves through divine resonance.
It is a divine response; it is neither I nor another. Thus it is said: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, appearing universally before all sentient beings.
Responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi.

When the resonance reaches even the most ignorant man or woman, only then is the resonance truly authentic. How could one not believe this? Furthermore, as for the principle of resonance, the Confucians...
He also spoke of this. The Master said: "If for one day one could overcome the self and return to ritual propriety (*li*), the whole world would turn to benevolence (*ren*).

From the time of King Zhou until now, more than two thousand years have passed; from the Son of Heaven and feudal lords down to all within the Middle Kingdom who speak of the Six Arts, they have taken the Master as their standard of judgment.
The divine resonance and divine response are likewise nothing more than this.
Someone asked about the doctrine of the three periods of existence, to which Guzi replied: "Within the realm there are two things: the Great Way and the Great Dharma. What is the Great Way?
It is the constant relations and ethical principles. This is what is meant by 'Heaven ordains the statutes' and 'Heaven ranks the rites'; it is rooted in humanity."
This is the spontaneous nature of the human heart, which cannot be otherwise.

If the teachings of the Buddha were put into practice, then all loyal ministers and filial sons would come to repay the kindness of their past lives, and all rebellious ministers and treacherous sons would come to repay the enmity of their past lives.
This is simply a matter of returning to the spontaneous nature of the human heart, which cannot be otherwise.
I see that they are no longer relevant. Consequently, the principles of the social order and human relations become hazy and lack any binding connection; thus, the Way is exhausted.

What constitutes the Great Law? It is the promotion of the worthy and the demotion of the unworthy, the granting of rewards and the imposition of punishments—what is called "Heaven’s mandate for the virtuous."
"Heaven punishes the guilty; this arises from what is naturally right in the human heart and cannot possibly be otherwise.

If the teachings of the Buddha were to prevail, then every gentleman who is subjected to execution or humiliation would be suffering the calamity of his own making, and those who execute or humiliate him would not be injuring the virtuous.
Likewise, every petty man who attains prominence and honor would be bringing this upon himself."
To cease [punishment] and instead grant honor and glory is not for the purpose of shielding evil. When measured against what is naturally appropriate to the human heart, there is no room for error;

I see that these two positions do not contradict one another. Thus, in matters of demotion or promotion, bestowal or withdrawal, if one acts with indifference and has no basis for judgment, the law reaches its limit.
Zhi Guizi said: "Within the dharma of causes and conditions, the fruits of retribution each differ. However...
The Buddha’s teaching of humanity rests solely upon the Dharma of the single mind. The three periods of time are fundamentally empty; causes and conditions are not inherently existent.
As for avoiding misfortune and pursuing good fortune, cultivating virtue and preventing wrongdoing—the cause is what must be feared, and the fruit is what cannot be escaped.

A loyal minister and a filial son who recognize kindness and repay it do so spontaneously, without deliberate effort; this is precisely where they find themselves compelled to act. As for a rebellious minister or a treacherous son—
To repay enmity with enmity is itself an insoluble knot; it places one under a sentence of no pardon.

When a gentleman suffers humiliation and execution, how could there not be a cause for such execution and humiliation? Yet the one who inflicts that humiliation and execution shall naturally receive the retribution for injuring the virtuous.
When a petty person receives manifest honor and glory, they ought to possess the merit for such honor and glory; yet, regarding this manifest honor...
Such a person cannot escape the punishment for harboring evil. Therefore, the integrity of a gentleman consists simply in acting according to his current station;
the law of a sovereign consists simply in clarifying the eternal Way. The essential point of the Three Ages does not lie outside the single mind;
the principle of causes and conditions does not depart from the present moment. As for [your claim that this] obstructs the Way and the Dharma, I do not understand it.
Guzi said: "Our Sage takes human relations as the actual reality.

What he calls 'mind-nature' exists precisely within the relationships of ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brothers, and husband and wife. The Buddhists regard human relations as illusory traces;

what they call 'mind-nature' lies outside of the relationships of ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brothers, and husband and wife. In ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brothers...

Within the relationship between husband and wife, this is called "the unity of essence and function" (*ti-yong yi-yuan*) and "the absence of interval between the manifest and the subtle" (*xian-wei wu-jian*).

Apart from the relationships of ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brothers, and husband and wife, essence and function, as well as the manifest and the subtle, would be split into two separate sections.

Even if one speaks word after word of this "unity of essence and function" and "absence of interval," can one truly achieve such unity and continuity? Zhiguizi said: "Nature has no interior or exterior."

The Way has neither interior nor exterior; it resides within the relationships of ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brother, and husband and wife, yet it does not dwell anywhere specific—it simply accords with and responds to them.

It is likewise present in that which is not comprised by these relationships of ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brother, and husband and wife, yet it is nowhere absent—it simply achieves itself in silence. This is called the unity of essence and function.
Originally, from the subtlest to the most manifest, there must be ruler and subject, father and son, elder and younger brother, and husband and wife before one can speak of the Way.
Thus, at the very beginning when human nature is born in its state of stillness, by what means shall the Way be realized?

Furthermore, during the present moment of neither seeing nor hearing, by what means shall the Way be realized? If we extend this reasoning to a time when even a single breath is not continuous, again, by what means shall [the Way be realized]?
What constitutes the Way? If we thus examine its origin and consider its culmination, looking back at the present moment, the occasions when one is separated from the Way are already many.
Can one ever remain in uninterrupted unity with its source? Therefore it is said: "The Way cannot be departed from for even a moment;
that which can be departed from is not the Way. One should recognize and grasp that which cannot be departed from.
Gaozi of Liang said: "The reason the learning of the sages differs from that of the Buddhists lies solely in the word 'nature' (xing).
The reason the sages' discourse on nature differs from the Buddhists' discourse on nature lies solely in the word 'principle' (li). Principle is Heaven..."
This is principle (*li*). "Celestial principle" refers to the natural order that exists spontaneously. Thus it is said: "Heaven ordains and Heaven ranks; Heaven commands and Heaven punishes.
In this regard, there is not even the slightest deviation, as fine as a needle's point. From the former sages to the later sages, the standard is one and the same.

This principle lies above the single thread of the "Plucking the Flower" (the transmission from Mahākāśyapa). It is not easy to speak of it unless one has exhausted the investigation of principle to its ultimate limit. To know where to return is the way.
The Master said: "Among the various Confucian scholars of the Song and Ming dynasties, there were many who debated the nature of the mind (xìngxīn).

For the most part, they bifurcated nature and mind, treating them as two distinct entities. There were also many who debated the relationship between principle (lǐ) and vital energy (qì). For the most part, they bifurcated principle and energy, treating them as two distinct entities.
The *Great Learning* speaks of the mind but does not speak of nature; nature is simply the mind. The *Doctrine of the Mean* speaks of nature..."
To speak of the mind (*citta*), the mind is itself the nature (*prakṛti*). In the *Great Changes* (*Da Yi*), principle (*li*) is discussed but not qi;
yet qi is itself principle. In Mencius, qi is discussed as the Way (*Dao*); qi is also the Way. To speak of them together, there is only the one mind.
For one who has realized the mind, even "one" does not stand; how much less could there be "two"? Those who perceive duality are all those who do not know the mind.
Furthermore, as for what Master Gao has said regarding the ultimate limit of exhausting principle (*li*): can it be known by means of knowledge, or recognized by means of cognition?
If it could be known by knowledge or recognized by cognition, then it would not be the primordial nature of Heaven’s creation; how, then, could it be called the ultimate limit?
It cannot be known by cognition, nor can it be recognized by consciousness. How does this differ from the single thread of the "Flower-holding" (Huānián) incident?
Does it, however, result in a distinction of high and low?
Gaozi said: "The followers of the Buddha level out good and evil, right and wrong, and speak of equality.

They certainly say there is no mind of discrimination, yet they possess a nature of discrimination. I, however, maintain that while there is a nature of discrimination, there is also a function of non-discrimination.
[If otherwise,] they would cause the world’s distinctions between good and evil, right and wrong, to become inverted and chaotic, leaving the entire age to rot and decay without regard."
"It is simply that they lack benevolence. Zhiguizi said: "The sun moves through the heavens;
those above it are like ridges and crags, and those below it are like ponds and pools, or even latrines—there is nowhere it does not illuminate. Water flows across the earth;

its small forms are like ditches and canals, and its large forms are like the Yangtze, the Huai, the Yellow River, and the oceans—there is nowhere it does not enter. Such is the nature of the sun and water."
Is it not that good and evil exist within this interval?

If there were good and evil within this interval, then the clarity [of the mind] would have long since ceased, and its flow would have quickly become obstructed. How great is equanimity! Is it not the very heart of Heaven?
Regarding Heaven’s dealings with humanity—whether in misfortune or fortune, rising or sinking, flourishing or withering, life or death—it does not create distinctions between them.
It is simply that one receives exactly what one has taken for oneself; it is merely a matter of equality.
One does not hear of [the Buddha] bringing the entire world to ruin, to rot, or to corruption. Furthermore, regarding right and wrong, good and evil, the Buddha’s regulations are strict:
the five precepts, the ten precepts, the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts, the two hundred and fifty precepts, and the five hundred precepts—these are the ultimate [standards].
Through its three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices, it leads all members of the fourfold assembly into the realm of purity.
Therefore, when remaining in the world, one becomes a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*), an elder (*śreṣṭhin*), or a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*);

when transcending the world, one becomes a *śrāvaka*, a *pratyekabuddha*, or a *bodhisattva*. Never has there been heard of anything that causes an entire generation to wither and rot like a pestilence.
It destroys them. Thus, while there is no discriminating mind, there is the functioning of discrimination;
this is precisely why the Buddha is the Buddha, why Heaven is Heaven, and also why the Sage is the Sage.
How great indeed is his benevolence!
Gaozi said: "In the principle of correspondence between Heaven and Earth, where there is yang, there must be yin; where there is our Confucianism, there must be the two other schools.

The teaching of the Buddhists is a yin teaching. One can see this generally by observing that they originated in the West, their doctrines were translated from foreign lands, and all that they speak concerns the matters of ghosts and spirits.
Since ancient times, in the most well-governed eras of the yang division, what [was the state of affairs]?"

It has been observed that when the influence of the Buddha flourishes to its utmost in the Yang, Yin begins to arise. During the era of the Three Dynasties, the world already belonged to the realm of Yin;
by the time of Confucius, my Way had reached its greatest height, yet Buddhism and Daoism subsequently emerged side-by-side within it.

As the fortunes of the age declined further and the sagely Way waned even more, the teachers of Buddhism and Daoism each, according to their own [capacity], presided over the instruction of the people.
[This is] a category [of teaching]. Zhiguizi said: "The two meanings of yin and yang are sometimes termed 'great' and 'small,' and sometimes metaphorically represented as 'good' and 'evil.

The Buddha-dharma cannot be measured by greatness or smallness, nor can it be compared to good or evil. Why then would it be a teaching of yin? Please allow me to investigate and explain this further.
The teaching of the Confucians takes the mandate of Heaven as its principle and takes ultimate goodness as its essence. Its position is—"
Heaven and Earth nurture all things as the myriad beings; this is simply the continuous process of life-giving, unceasingly so.
It is simply the state of ultimate sincerity without interruption. Because its mechanism is compliant, its function always resides in governing the world.

The teaching of Laozi takes non-action (*wuji*) as its principle and the subtle and ineffable (*xīyíwēi*) as its essence. By diminishing and further diminishing, one arrives at non-action (*wúwéi*). Non-action...
Yet there is nothing it does not accomplish. Its mechanism is contrary yet compliant; thus its application extends to both the mundane and the supramundane.

The teaching of the Buddha takes the one mind as its fundamental principle and the exhaustion of all space and pervasion of the Dharma-realm as its essence. It is form and yet emptiness; it is neither emptiness nor form.
It transcends the four marks and emerges from the three realms of existence. Because its mechanism is contrary, its path always prioritizes the supramundane.
However, when it is said that "Heaven bears all things," taking the absence of sound and smell as the ultimate, then the Great Ultimate (Tài jí) would revert to the Poleless (Wújí).

When it is said, "What do I know? I know nothing," one transcends both form and emptiness. Ultimately, from the perspective of the original source, neither nirvana nor birth-and-death can be apprehended.
What is favorable? What is adverse? It is neither mundane nor supramundane; it is one and the same.
The Ocean of Wondrous Adornments of Vairocana. Alas! Who is sufficient to grasp its meaning, were it not for one who contemplates the vast and luminous source?
As for taking offense at the Western foreign lands—is King Wen not himself a man from the West?
Furthermore, the discourse on ghosts and spirits appears repeatedly in the *Shi* and *Shu*; what, then, can be said of this? Regarding the Three Dynasties...
As for the claim that the world belongs to the Yin principle, this is not a comprehensive argument. Disorder and order cycle one another, and Yin and Yang alternate in their movements.

When considering the reigns of Emperor Ming of the Han, Taizong of the Tang, and Taizu of the Ming, which of these were more orderly than those of the Spring and Autumn period? Yet Buddhism flourished during them.
Is this truly summoned by the Yin?
Someone asked Zhiguī, saying, "You, sir, are a Confucianist. You have long been accustomed to the books of the various masters.
Now that you abandon them for Buddhism, will this not be a betrayal of your roots? He replied, "What I speak of is the public discourse of the world;
it is not something I may claim as my own private possession. The Buddha-dharma has circulated in the world for a long time; it is a bridge and a causeway across the sea of suffering."
It is the eye of all sentient beings; it is that which the celestial emperors protect and the spirits and ghosts revere.
The Six Heretics could not obstruct its transformation, and the three Wu emperors could not stem its flow.
Yet these various masters now wish to reject and refute it based on their parochial views; this is merely labor with little merit. As for those who would refute it:
Some consider it a false teaching; others consider it a heterodox sect. To consider it a heterodox sect means that attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been forgotten.
To consider it a false teaching means that the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) has not yet been attained.

As for the various masters of today, they have certainly forgotten their attachment to dharmas and have attained the divine eye. Thus, what I have said is precisely what all these masters ought to say. Furthermore...
What difference does it make? Furthermore, the achievements of the various masters are truly not easy to fathom. When Gaozi entered the Way, he read the words of Cheng Bozi, which say:
"The myriad transformations all reside in the person; in reality, there is not a single thing. He then attained a decisive realization, saying:
"In reality, from the beginning, there has never been a single thing. Later, in a letter to others, he wrote: "The mind is like the great void; its essence..."
"There is no birth and death. How remarkably his words resemble those of the Buddha! Is it only Gaozi? Lu Jiuyuan’s words say:
"Without conscious knowledge, follow the pattern of the Lord. Does this principle admit of conscious knowledge? "What do I have that I could know?
